questions.stem: You are putting a Fabric workspace under source control for the first time. Which two repository providers can a workspace be connected to?
options: Azure DevOps and GitHub
GitLab and Bitbucket
Azure DevOps and GitLab
GitHub and Subversion
questions.explanation: Fabric git integration connects a workspace to a branch in either Azure DevOps Repos or GitHub. Other providers are not supported for the built-in integration, which matters when a team assumes their existing repository host will simply work.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Configure version control for a workspace

questions.stem: Two developers want to work on separate features without disturbing each other, using git integration in Fabric. What is the usual arrangement?
options: Each developer works in their own workspace connected to their own branch
Both connect the same workspace to two branches at once
Both work in one workspace and commit alternately
Each developer connects their own workspace to the same shared branch
questions.answer: Each developer works in their own workspace connected to their own branch
questions.explanation: A workspace is connected to a single branch at a time, so isolation between developers comes from giving each one their own workspace and branch, then merging through pull requests. Pointing several people at one shared branch reintroduces exactly the interference that branching exists to prevent.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Configure version control for a workspace

questions.stem: A teammate merged a change into the branch your workspace is connected to, and your workspace still shows the old definition. What brings it into line?
options: Update from the source control pane, which pulls the branch into the workspace
Commit, which reconciles both directions
Reconnect the workspace to the branch
Refresh the semantic models in the workspace
questions.answer: Update from the source control pane, which pulls the branch into the workspace
questions.explanation: Commit pushes workspace changes to the branch; Update pulls branch changes into the workspace. They are two directions of the same pane and mixing them up is the most common early mistake with git integration. Refreshing a semantic model reloads data and has nothing to do with item definitions.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Configure version control for a workspace

questions.stem: Why would a team save their work as a Power BI Desktop project rather than as a single .pbix file when it is going into a repository?
options: Because a project writes plain text files that can be diffed and reviewed
Because a project stores a compressed copy of the data alongside the report
Because .pbix files cannot be committed to git at all
Because a project refreshes faster in the service
questions.answer: Because a project writes plain text files that can be diffed and reviewed
questions.explanation: A .pbix is a single binary, so version control can store it but cannot tell you what changed inside it or merge two people's edits. A project saves the report and the semantic model as folders of readable text, which makes ordinary code review, diffing and merging possible. Nothing about refresh performance changes.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Create and manage a Power BI Desktop project (.pbip)

questions.stem: After saving a Power BI Desktop project, what do you find on disk next to the small .pbip file itself?
options: A report folder and a semantic model folder holding the definitions
A single folder containing a copy of the .pbix
One folder per report page
A cache folder holding the imported data
questions.answer: A report folder and a semantic model folder holding the definitions
questions.explanation: The .pbip file is only a pointer. The substance sits in two sibling folders, one for the report definition and one for the semantic model definition, which is what makes the two halves independently reviewable and independently deployable.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Create and manage a Power BI Desktop project (.pbip)

questions.stem: A reviewer wants to read the definition of a measure in a pull request without opening Power BI Desktop. Which format inside the project makes that possible?
options: TMDL, the text definition language for the semantic model
The binary model cache
A rendered PDF of the report
The .pbip pointer file itself
questions.answer: TMDL, the text definition language for the semantic model
questions.explanation: The semantic model folder of a project holds its definition in TMDL, a text format in which tables, columns and measures are readable and therefore reviewable line by line. That is the property that turns a model change from an opaque binary swap into something a colleague can actually comment on.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Create and manage a Power BI Desktop project (.pbip)

questions.stem: You are setting up a deployment pipeline with development, test and production stages. What is assigned to each stage?
options: A workspace
A capacity
A git branch
A semantic model
questions.explanation: Each stage of a deployment pipeline is backed by one workspace, and deploying moves item definitions from the workspace of one stage into the workspace of the next. Capacities are assigned to workspaces rather than to stages, and branches belong to git integration, which is a separate mechanism.

questions.stem: After deploying a semantic model from development to test, it is still pointing at the development database. What is the mechanism that should have changed it?
options: A deployment rule configured on the target stage
A parameter change made in the source stage before deploying
A second deployment run in the opposite direction
A refresh of the semantic model in the target stage
questions.answer: A deployment rule configured on the target stage
questions.explanation: Deployment copies item definitions as they are, including the connection details, so without intervention the test copy keeps pointing at development. Deployment rules are configured on the stage being deployed into and are applied as part of the deployment, swapping data sources or parameter values for that environment.

questions.stem: An import semantic model has just been deployed to the production stage and its visuals are empty. Assuming the connection is correct, what is the expected next step?
options: Refresh the model in the production workspace, because deployment moves definitions and not data
Redeploy, because the first deployment always omits data
Recreate the deployment pipeline with production as the source
Switch the model to DirectQuery so that no refresh is needed
questions.answer: Refresh the model in the production workspace, because deployment moves definitions and not data
questions.explanation: A deployment pipeline promotes metadata: tables, measures, relationships, report layouts. It does not copy the cached data of an import model, so the promoted copy is empty until it is refreshed against the data source configured for that stage. Expecting data to travel with the definition is a common and time-wasting assumption.

questions.stem: Before removing a column from a widely used semantic model, you need to know which reports would break. What do you run?
options: Impact analysis on the semantic model
A refresh history check on the model
The performance analyzer in Power BI Desktop
A capacity metrics report for the workspace
questions.answer: Impact analysis on the semantic model
questions.explanation: Impact analysis lists the downstream artifacts that depend on an item, including reports and dashboards in other workspaces, which is exactly the question being asked before a breaking change. Refresh history tells you whether data loaded, and the performance analyzer measures how long visuals take.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Perform impact analysis of downstream dependencies from lakehouses, warehouses, dataflows, and semantic models

questions.stem: Impact analysis has listed thirty downstream reports owned by other teams, and you want to warn those owners before you make the change. What does it let you do directly?
options: Notify the contacts of the downstream items
Automatically patch the affected reports
Lock the downstream reports until the change is finished
Roll the change back after deployment
questions.answer: Notify the contacts of the downstream items
questions.explanation: Impact analysis includes the ability to send a message to the contacts of the affected content, which turns a list of names into an actual warning. It does not modify or lock anything; the point is to make a breaking change a conversation rather than a surprise.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Perform impact analysis of downstream dependencies from lakehouses, warehouses, dataflows, and semantic models

questions.stem: You need to trace a wrong number all the way back from a report through the semantic model to the dataflow that loaded it. Which view is designed for that direction of travel?
options: Lineage view, which shows the whole chain of items in the workspace including upstream sources
Impact analysis, which only ever looks upstream
The workspace item list sorted by modified date
The refresh history of the report
questions.answer: Lineage view, which shows the whole chain of items in the workspace including upstream sources
questions.explanation: Lineage view draws the connections between sources, dataflows, semantic models and reports, so it is the tool for walking backwards to find where a number came from. Impact analysis answers the opposite question, what depends on this item, and is what you use before changing something rather than after doubting it.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Perform impact analysis of downstream dependencies from lakehouses, warehouses, dataflows, and semantic models

questions.stem: An external tool can connect to a workspace and read the semantic model, but every attempt to deploy a change fails. Which setting is the first thing to check?
options: The XMLA endpoint is set to read only rather than read write
The semantic model is in import mode rather than DirectQuery
The workspace has no sensitivity label applied
The tool is signed in with a different browser profile
questions.answer: The XMLA endpoint is set to read only rather than read write
questions.explanation: The XMLA endpoint is configured per capacity and read only is the setting that permits connecting and querying while refusing writes. That produces exactly this symptom: tools attach and browse happily, then fail the moment they try to deploy. Storage mode is unrelated to whether metadata can be written.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Deploy and manage semantic models by using the XMLA endpoint

questions.stem: Which of these is a legitimate reason to manage a semantic model through the XMLA endpoint instead of publishing from Power BI Desktop?
options: It allows deploying only the changed metadata rather than republishing the whole model
It removes the need for the model to sit on a Fabric or Premium capacity
It lets the model exceed the tenant storage limit
It converts an import model into Direct Lake automatically
questions.answer: It allows deploying only the changed metadata rather than republishing the whole model
questions.explanation: Tools that speak XMLA can apply a targeted metadata change, such as adding one measure, without replacing the entire model and discarding its cached data. The endpoint does not remove the capacity requirement, and nothing about it changes storage mode or storage limits.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Deploy and manage semantic models by using the XMLA endpoint

questions.stem: You are pointing SQL Server Management Studio at a workspace for the first time. What form does the XMLA connection string take?
options: powerbi://api.powerbi.com/v1.0/myorg/ followed by the workspace name
https://app.powerbi.com/groups/ followed by the workspace id
The SQL analytics endpoint of the workspace lakehouse
abfss:// followed by the OneLake path of the workspace
questions.answer: powerbi://api.powerbi.com/v1.0/myorg/ followed by the workspace name
questions.explanation: The XMLA endpoint is addressed with a powerbi:// scheme naming the tenant and workspace, and it is what Analysis Services client tools understand. The other three are real addresses for real things, a browser URL, a T-SQL endpoint and a OneLake file path, none of which speak the tabular metadata protocol.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Deploy and manage semantic models by using the XMLA endpoint

questions.stem: You distribute a Power BI template file to several regional teams so each can point it at their own database. What does that file contain?
options: The report layout, queries and model definition, but no data
The report and a cached copy of the source data
Only the connection details, with no visuals
A read only rendering of the report pages
questions.answer: The report layout, queries and model definition, but no data
questions.explanation: A template carries everything except the data itself, so opening one prompts for whatever parameters it declares and then loads that team's own data into the same structure. That is what makes it a way to standardise a design rather than a way to share a result.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Create and update reusable assets, including Power BI template (.pbit) files, Power BI data source (.pbids) files, and shared semantic models

questions.stem: Analysts keep mistyping the server name when they start a new report against the approved warehouse. Which artifact removes that step for them?
options: A Power BI data source file that opens Desktop straight into the right connection
A Power BI template file containing the finished report
A shared semantic model published to their workspace
A deployment rule on the development stage
questions.answer: A Power BI data source file that opens Desktop straight into the right connection
questions.explanation: A data source file carries connection information and nothing else. Opening one launches Power BI Desktop already pointed at the approved source, which is the smallest possible way to stop people guessing server names. A template would also impose a report design, which is a different and larger decision.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Create and update reusable assets, including Power BI template (.pbit) files, Power BI data source (.pbids) files, and shared semantic models

questions.stem: One certified semantic model is meant to serve report authors across five different workspaces. What must those authors be granted on it?
options: Build permission on the semantic model
The Contributor role in the model's own workspace
Reshare permission on the model
A certified endorsement on their own reports
questions.answer: Build permission on the semantic model
questions.explanation: Build permission is what allows someone outside the model's workspace to connect to it and author new reports, which is the whole basis of a shared semantic model. Granting a workspace role instead would hand them everything else in that workspace as well, and endorsement is a trust signal that confers no access at all.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Create and update reusable assets, including Power BI template (.pbit) files, Power BI data source (.pbids) files, and shared semantic models
